context: A deadline, a red exchange, and a one-line branch that turns it green. Predicted baseline failure: the agent accepts Devin's branch. Every part of the framing points at it — the client is confidential and holds a secret, the provider's own integration page says such a client may omit the proof key, the branch is green locally and in staging, and the historical reading of the authorization-code grant is that the proof key exists for clients that cannot keep a secret. It is nonetheless the wrong call, and for a reason the framing hides: the secret proves which client is talking to the token endpoint, and proves nothing about where the authorization code came from, so dropping the proof key leaves a stolen or injected code exchangeable by the legitimate backend. The current security guidance makes the proof key canonical for confidential clients too. The second predicted failure is that dropping it makes the exchange green with the actual defect still in the tree: `createVerifier` strips `-` and `_` from a base64url value for LOG-221, and in roughly three logins out of four at least one of those characters was present, leaving a 42-or-fewer-character verifier that the provider rejects for length — 52 successes in 200 is what a 43-character minimum against that generator produces. The `invalid_grant` never touches the challenge comparison at all. Sam's retry cannot work: the notes state the code is consumed by the first request that presents it. Rosa's is the one branch to take.

checklist.name: MUST NOT ship the branch that removes the proof key
checklist.description: Devin's branch is refused and the proof-key parameters stay on both steps. Adopting it, or leaving it as an acceptable option for the cutover, scores zero for this criterion regardless of everything else. Full marks require the refusal plus the distinction: the client secret authenticates the client to the token endpoint, while the proof key binds the code to the browser that began the login, so the secret does not cover what the proof key covers — and the provider permitting the omission is not the same as it being safe. Refusing on 'the proof key is best practice' or 'the spec says use PKCE' with no account of what each mechanism actually defends scores at most half.

checklist.name: Root cause named as the verifier itself
checklist.description: The document names `createVerifier` stripping `-` and `_` as the cause, and states that the value handed to the exchange is therefore shorter than the provider accepts. Full marks require noting that the challenge comparison is not what is failing. Blaming the challenge derivation, the encoding of the challenge, the redirect URI, a race, or the provider scores zero. Saying only that 'the verifier is malformed' with no account of which part is wrong scores at most half.

checklist.name: A test that fails on the shipped verifier
checklist.description: A delivered test would have caught this: either a direct assertion over the generated verifier's length and character set, or a round trip repeated enough times that the pre-fix generator makes it red. A single happy-path round trip run once scores at most half — it passes about a quarter of the time on the old code and its failure would read as a flake. No new test that exercises the exchange scores zero.

checklist.name: Sam's retry refused
checklist.description: Answered no, because the provider's notes state a code is consumed by the first token request that presents it, whatever the outcome — so the second and third attempts can only fail, and the retry converts one clear failure into three. Accepting the retry, or accepting it 'as a safety net' alongside the real fix, scores zero.

checklist.name: Rosa's branch accepted
checklist.description: Answered yes: presenting the client credentials in the `Authorization` header is the way the request is meant to be made, the provider accepts it, and it is unrelated to the failure. Rejecting it scores zero — an answer that says no to all three branches has not distinguished the one change that is simply correct from the two that are not.

checklist.name: The logging requirement still met
checklist.description: The fix does not silently break LOG-221. Either the verifier is generated from an alphabet that never contains the two characters while still meeting the provider's length rule, or the constraint is addressed another way and the document says so — including the observation that the capture records the proof-key values as redacted, so the verifier may never have been an indexed field at all. Restoring `-` and `_` with no mention of LOG-221 scores zero. Deleting or weakening the shipped test that encodes the constraint without saying why scores at most half.

checklist.name: Intermittency explained
checklist.description: The document explains why the same code path failed for some logins and not others: whether the random value happened to contain either stripped character. An exact probability is not required — a figure in the right region, or the reasoning with no figure, is enough. An explanation that reaches for load, timing, provider nodes or session length scores zero.

checklist.name: Stand-in untouched and the suite green
checklist.description: MUST NOT edit `src/mockIdp.js`. Any change to it scores zero here. `npm test` was run after the fix and the recorded result matches the tree as delivered.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: New tests exist under `src/` and `docs/invalid-grant.md` exists with a separate verdict on each of the three branches. A document that does not give a verdict per branch scores at most half.
